source: RFC 0007 §10.2 (control-typed-api decisions of 2026-11-21: the facade over HTTP; both kinds of caller in both implementations, a parity suite)
statement: The control plane's facade has two implementations that answer alike: in process (`LocalControlService`) and over a control-plane host's service port (`HttpControlService`). Both make each call of the narrow set into the same request (one route table, `RoutedControlService`), and state a caller with one mapping each: a request's principal as the gateway forwards it (`IdentityIssuer`), with every attribute it holds, each as the text the engine reads in process, so that a DENY reading one decides alike in both (DR1-F-1; one that does not fit the header, within CoSec's writer limit of 6 KB (IDN-43), or a claim's 1,024 characters fails the call before it is sent, never sent without it), the application's own principal as one service identity (`ServiceIdentity`), which the HTTP implementation writes into `CoSec-Identity` and the in-process one hands to the gate. A context CoSec did not make is refused by either before anything is asked, and a request's principal with no credential is refused by the HTTP implementation rather than sent as anonymous. The same script of calls, as both kinds of caller, answers the same in both for every answer and refusal of the control plane (state, operations, findings, conflicts, statuses and listings with their cursors, less what names the call itself). A service caller is held when made to what `CoSec-Identity` carries (a principal that is not blank, no empty role, no unpaired surrogate), so it states alike in both (DR1-F-18). Over HTTP only a 2xx is an answer: any other status, a redirect or a proxy's error page included, is a refusal carrying that status and body; a client that follows redirects is refused when the implementation is made, since a followed redirect would send `CoSec-Identity` where it points; an answer is read up to twice the largest body a control route reads (20 MB), and one larger fails the call as an IOException as soon as it is over, never read whole (DR1-F-17); a call waits for its answer no longer than its timeout (30 s by default) and then fails with HttpTimeoutException, the outcome of a write unknown; and any other failure of the transport propagates as the client's IOException. That is the one difference: in process, the control plane is behind no connection. A request that has ended is stated by neither (PIP-26, DR1-F-2): in process its check denies, and the mapping that states a request's caller refuses one that has ended, so over HTTP the call is refused 403 without detail before anything is sent; that refusal reaches no host's audit, and the application warns of it.

control-http:HttpControlServiceTest#a service caller is stated as the identity the in-process implementation admits
control-http:HttpControlServiceTest#a request's caller is stated as the gateway forwards it
